Roots and Resilience: How Family Adversity Shapes Child and Adult Outcomes

Maliha

2026-06-03

Introduction

This project explores how adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) — particularly parental depression and household dysfunction — shape child and adult outcomes, and what factors predict resilience.

Depression Distribution

NHANES %>%
  filter(!is.na(Depressed)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Depressed, fill = Depressed)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "Depression Frequency in NHANES Sample",
    x = "Depressed (Days in past 2 weeks)",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Majority report no depression — expected But ~1000 report “Several” days and ~450 report “Most” days That’s roughly 1 in 7 people in this sample experiencing significant depressive symptoms

That’s not a small signal. That’s a public health pattern. Adding poverty: Depression by Poverty Level

NHANES %>%
  filter(!is.na(Depressed), !is.na(Poverty)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Depressed, y = Poverty, fill = Depressed)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Poverty Level by Depression Severity",
    x = "Depression Frequency",
    y = "Poverty Index (lower = more poverty)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

What this shows:

“None” group — median poverty index ~3.3 (more resources) “Several” group — median drops to ~2.3 “Most” group — median drops further to ~1.4 (closest to poverty line)

The pattern is clear and consistent — as depression severity increases, poverty index decreases. More depression, fewer resources. Every step of the gradient moves in the same direction. That’s not noise. That’s a signal worth writing about.

Finding 1: Poverty and Depression Move Together

Analysis of the NHANES sample reveals a consistent gradient between economic hardship and depression severity. Individuals reporting depressive symptoms “most” days show markedly lower poverty index scores compared to those reporting none, suggesting that financial stress and mental health burden are deeply intertwined — not independent risk factors.

NHANES %>%
  filter(!is.na(Depressed), !is.na(SleepTrouble)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Depressed, fill = SleepTrouble)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "Sleep Trouble by Depression Severity",
    x = "Depression Frequency",
    y = "Proportion",
    fill = "Sleep Trouble"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

What this shows:

“None” group — ~20% report sleep trouble “Several” group — jumps to ~38% “Most” group — crosses 50%. More than half report sleep trouble

The gradient holds again. Every step up in depression severity brings more sleep disruption. And that 50% threshold in the “Most” group is striking — sleep trouble stops being a symptom and starts looking like a co-condition.

Finding 2: Sleep Disruption Scales with Depression Severity

Among those reporting depressive symptoms most days, over half also report trouble sleeping — more than double the rate seen in those with no depression. This pattern suggests sleep disruption is not merely a side effect but a compounding factor in severe depression, potentially creating a reinforcing cycle of poor mental health and physical dysregulation.

NHANES %>%
  filter(!is.na(Depressed), !is.na(PhysActive)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Depressed, fill = PhysActive)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "Physical Activity by Depression Severity",
    x = "Depression Frequency",
    y = "Proportion",
    fill = "Physically Active"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

first resilience finding. What this shows:

“None” group — ~58% are physically active “Several” group — drops to ~47% “Most” group — drops to ~34%

The gradient flips. As depression gets worse, physical activity decreases. Or framed the other way — physical activity is consistently more present in the less depressed group. This is your first answer to what gets people out — or at least what looks different in people who aren’t stuck.

Finding 3: Physical Activity as a Protective Factor

Physical activity follows a clear inverse relationship with depression severity. Nearly 6 in 10 people reporting no depression are physically active, compared to only 1 in 3 among those experiencing depressive symptoms most days. While causality cannot be established from this data alone, the pattern is consistent with research suggesting movement as a meaningful protective factor against depression.

Finding 1: Poverty and depression move together Finding 2: Sleep disruption scales with severity Finding 3: Physical activity is protective

Gender and Depression

NHANES %>%
  filter(!is.na(Depressed), !is.na(Gender)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Depressed, fill = Gender)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "Depression Severity by Gender",
    x = "Depression Frequency",
    y = "Proportion",
    fill = "Gender"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

What this shows:

“None” group — roughly 50/50 male/female, slightly more male “Several” group — shifts to ~55% female “Most” group — shifts further to ~60% female

As depression severity increases, women are increasingly overrepresented. Men don’t disappear from the severe group — but the gender gap widens at every step.

Finding 4: Gender and Depression Severity

Women are disproportionately represented among those experiencing the most severe depressive symptoms. While the sample is roughly equal by gender overall, women account for nearly 60% of those reporting depressive feelings most days. This pattern is consistent with well-documented gender disparities in depression prevalence and raises important questions about the structural, biological, and social factors that place women at higher risk — including caregiving burden, economic inequality, and hormonal vulnerability.

the seed for Project 2: The biological angle is genuinely rich territory. Possible question: “How do biological markers — cortisol, inflammation, hormonal patterns — differ across depression severity, and do they interact with gender?” NHANES actually has some biological variables already — testosterone, cholesterol. for deeper biology:

NHANES lab files — includes CRP (inflammation marker), cortisol proxies UK Biobank — massive, includes genetics, biological assays, mental health ABCD Study — brain imaging + family environment + child outcomes

4 findings:

Poverty and depression move together Sleep disruption scales with severity Physical activity is protective Women are overrepresented in severe depression

Conclusion

# Summary of key findings

What This Analysis Shows

This exploratory analysis of NHANES data reveals a consistent, multi-layered portrait of depression in the US adult population. Economic hardship, sleep disruption, physical inactivity, and gender each independently track with depression severity — and likely interact with one another in ways this cross-sectional data cannot fully capture.

What This Analysis Cannot Tell Us

Causality. This data is a snapshot, not a timeline. We cannot say poverty causes depression, or that inactivity leads to worse outcomes — only that they co-occur in a meaningful pattern. Longitudinal data would be required to establish direction.

What Comes Next

Project 2 will examine biological markers — inflammation, hormonal patterns, and physiological stress responses — and their relationship to depression severity and gender. Using NHANES lab files and potentially UK Biobank data, the goal is to move beyond behavioral correlates into the biological substrates of what keeps people stuck.

Summary: How All Factors Relate

library(reshape2)
## 
## Attaching package: 'reshape2'
## The following object is masked from 'package:tidyr':
## 
##     smiths
# Create numeric version of key variables
nhanes_numeric <- NHANES %>%
  filter(!is.na(Depressed), !is.na(Poverty), 
         !is.na(SleepTrouble), !is.na(PhysActive),
         !is.na(Gender)) %>%
  mutate(
    Depressed_n = as.numeric(Depressed),
    SleepTrouble_n = ifelse(SleepTrouble == "Yes", 1, 0),
    PhysActive_n = ifelse(PhysActive == "Yes", 1, 0),
    Gender_n = ifelse(Gender == "female", 1, 0)
  ) %>%
  select(
    Depression = Depressed_n,
    Poverty = Poverty,
    Sleep_Trouble = SleepTrouble_n,
    Physical_Activity = PhysActive_n,
    Gender_Female = Gender_n,
    Age = Age,
    HH_Income = HHIncomeMid
  )

# Correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(nhanes_numeric, use = "complete.obs")

# Melt and plot
melted_cor <- melt(cor_matrix)

ggplot(melted_cor, aes(x = Var1, y = Var2, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "tomato",
    midpoint = 0, limit = c(-1, 1),
    name = "Correlation"
  ) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(value, 2)), size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation Matrix: Depression and Associated Factors",
    x = "", y = ""
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

What to read here: Depression row (bottom):

Sleep_Trouble: +0.21 — strongest positive relationship. More sleep trouble, more depression Poverty: -0.19 — lower poverty index (more poverty), more depression HH_Income: -0.18 — lower income, more depression Physical_Activity: -0.11 — less activity, more depression Gender_Female: +0.07 — small but present female skew Age: -0.02 — essentially no relationship

The bonus finding — Poverty and HH_Income: +0.88 That’s expected — they measure similar things. Actually validates your data is clean.

Finding 5: Summary — What Matters Most

The correlation matrix confirms and quantifies the patterns observed throughout this analysis. Sleep trouble shows the strongest individual relationship with depression (r = 0.21), followed closely by poverty (r = -0.19) and household income (r = -0.18). Physical activity shows a modest protective relationship (r = -0.11). Gender shows a small but consistent female skew (r = 0.07).

Notably, no single factor dominates. Depression appears to be distributed across multiple compounding burdens — economic, physiological, and behavioral — rather than driven by any one cause. This has direct implications for intervention: addressing only one factor may be insufficient.
